blocks.text: Where a help desk technician's day actually goes

The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists the core duties of this job. You diagnose problems, record what users tell you and walk them through fixes. You also set up or repair equipment, install software, train people and report recurring problems to managers. Most of those steps happen mid-conversation, with someone who is already annoyed and waiting.

Public numbers on how a help desk day splits up are thin. The closest figure comes from SysAid, a vendor. Its survey of 718 IT professionals found that the average IT team loses 35% of its working time to manual, repetitive tasks. Treat that as a rough signal, not a measurement of your queue. The survey does not define what counts as a manual task.

The wider office research points the same way. A Microsoft Research study followed 40 information workers over 12 workdays. Longer daily time on email went with lower perceived productivity and higher stress. The same paper found no evidence that batching email lowers stress. Asana's survey puts 'work about work' at 60% of time, but that is vendor data about office workers, not technicians.
In practice, the time usually goes to five places:

items: Repeat fixes: password resets, Wi-Fi profiles and printer queues come back every week.
Searching: you hunt for the menu, the setting or the policy you used last month.
Switching apps: the ticket, the chat, the remote session and the notes all want you.
Writing: ticket notes, user replies and status updates often take longer than the fix.
Chasing status: you wait on a user, a manager or a colleague before the next step.

blocks.text: Why Mac tickets take longer than they should

Mac support has a naming problem. Apple renamed System Preferences to System Settings, and older guides still use the old name. Apple Remote Desktop, the main remote-support tool for Macs, is at version 3.10. It costs $79.99 on the Mac App Store and needs macOS 15.5 or later. Its newest features, including VoiceOver control of a remote Mac, need macOS Tahoe 26 or later.

blocks.title: Match the labels on your screen
blocks.text: If a guide says System Preferences > Sharing, current macOS uses System Settings > General > Sharing. Trust the label you can see. Old guides are useful for the steps, but the names may have moved.

Turning on Remote Management is the step most technicians look up twice. On current macOS, the path is Apple menu > System Settings > General > Sharing. Click the Info button next to Remote Management, turn it on, then set the Allow access for pop-up menu. That menu decides which users can connect. Set it on purpose.
How an AI assistant for IT help desk technicians fits into your shift

An AI assistant for IT help desk technicians works on the screen you already have open. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold ⌥ ⌘. When you ask where something is, it draws a circle and a label around it. When you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It does not click for you.
Worked example: turning on Remote Management with Lazur guiding you
Say a user cannot share their screen with you. Their Mac is on macOS Tahoe, and the request fails on their end. Here is how the session can go. You stay in control of every change.

items: Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to walk you through turning on Remote Management. It points at the Apple menu first.
Open System Settings, then go to General > Sharing. Lazur waits until the Sharing pane is on screen.
Click the Info button next to Remote Management and turn the switch on.
Set Allow access for to the users you need.
If a lock icon shows, you may need an admin name and password. Apple's older guide says so.
Ask the user to send the request again. Confirm it arrives before you close the ticket.

blocks.text: Two edge cases trip people up. Apple's guide says you may need to turn Remote Management off and on again before Screen Sharing fully works. The command line has limits too. The kickstart command gives view-only access on macOS 10.14 or later. From macOS 12.1, kickstart cannot enable Screen Sharing, and Apple recommends an MDM solution for those versions.

Screen Sharing has its own gate. In the Screen Sharing app, open Settings > Blocked Users. The 'Allow screen sharing requests from' pop-up lets you accept requests from anyone with an Apple Account, or only from contacts. You can also block specific Apple Accounts there. Check that setting when a user says a request never arrives.

blocks.text: The split matters most when a fix touches a user's data or access. Lazur can explain a setting in seconds. You still own the change, the record of it and the call to make it.
Writing ticket notes and replies without losing the afternoon

Writing takes more of the day than most people plan for. The Microsoft Research team linked long daily email time to lower perceived productivity and higher stress. Batching email did not show lower stress in that study. So the fix is not only a better inbox schedule. It is writing faster, without leaving the window you already have open.

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Snippets save text you type every day, such as a closing line or the steps you send most often. A personal dictionary helps with product names and odd spellings. Clipboard slots keep a few pieces of text ready to paste.
A ticket note that a colleague can use tomorrow has five parts:

items: Symptom: what the user sees, in their own words.
Environment: the macOS version, the Mac model and the app that failed.
Checks: what you looked at and what you ruled out.
Change: what you changed, and where you clicked.
Next step: who acts next, and when.

blocks.title: Check your data rules first
blocks.text: Ticket notes often hold employee names, serial numbers and access details. Follow your employer's rules on what can go into an AI tool. Lazur sends audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer. Those are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Ask your security team before you paste regulated data anywhere.
Research and quick questions between tickets

Some questions eat a long browsing session. What is the current Apple Remote Desktop version? Which macOS version does a feature need? Lazur can run that research in its own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It comes back with a summary and a report. Open the sources yourself before you repeat a number to a user.
If the ticket is about Chrome itself, see [Chrome for IT support technicians on Mac](/for/it-support-technicians/chrome). It covers policies, enrollment and clearing cache.
A Slack thread about a failed screen share

Users often report problems in Slack, where a short message is easy to answer badly. Read the whole thread, check the two Sharing settings, then reply with steps the user can follow. The demo on this page shows Lazur drafting that reply in the thread. You read it, change what you need and send it yourself. If Slack itself acts up, see [how to fix missing notifications in Slack on Mac](/how-to/fix-missing-notifications-in-slack).
Mistakes that waste the time you were trying to save

items: Trusting an old menu name. Match the labels on the screen in front of you.
Asking a vague question. Name the app and the setting, and Lazur can point at the right place.
Turning on sharing without checking who can send requests. Check the Screen Sharing settings too.
Skipping the lock icon. An admin name and password may be needed before a setting changes.
Pasting a whole ticket into any AI tool. Remove names and IDs unless your employer's rules allow them.

blocks.text: The first two mistakes cost the most time, because they send you hunting through the wrong pane. Check the label, then check the setting, in that order.
What to do next on your first shift with Lazur

Start small. Pick one repeated ticket this week, such as a Wi-Fi profile fix or a Remote Management check you look up often. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to walk you through it. Time the session against your usual route. Then decide whether the assistant earns a place in your shift.

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. You can [download the app](/download) and check the [pricing page](/pricing) for plans. A free trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card.

faq.question: Does Lazur click buttons or fix problems for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points at things, answers out loud and guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click before it moves on.

faq.question: Which Macs does Lazur run on?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. A Windows version is planned, but it is not available yet.

faq.question: When does Lazur look at my screen?
faq.answer: Only while you hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask a question. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with employee or customer data?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. This page does not make compliance claims for any industry. If you handle regulated data, ask your security team before you use an AI tool with it.

faq.question: Does Lazur run Apple Remote Desktop for me?
faq.answer: No. Ask Lazur how to set up Apple Remote Desktop, and it guides you through each step. Apple Remote Desktop 3.10 costs $79.99 on the Mac App Store and needs macOS 15.5 or later.

faq.question: Why does the menu on my Mac not match the guide?
faq.answer: Apple renamed System Preferences to System Settings. Older guides still use the old name. Match the labels on your screen, and ask Lazur to point at the right one.

faq.question: Does Lazur write the ticket for me?
faq.answer: It can draft text and type it at your cursor, or take dictation. You check the facts, edit the wording and save the ticket. The decision and the record stay with you.

faq.question: Does Lazur remember what I asked?
faq.answer: Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did. That memory is kept on your Mac.

faq.question: Which page should I read for Chrome problems?
faq.answer: Read [Chrome for IT support technicians on Mac](/for/it-support-technicians/chrome). It covers policies, enrollment and clearing cache.
